own_scenes.place: Santa Bárbara, Los Ángeles y Austin
own_scenes.desc: «The Third Eye» de los Dovers (abril de 1966) es uno de los primeros intentos de reproducir el viaje de LSD en un disco y de los más exactos: fanfarria oriental, drones a lo Ravi Shankar, doce cuerdas de raga, melodía horizontal sin cambios de acorde, voz de «místico punk» y una espiral casi fuera de control. Dura 135 segundos pero condensa una experiencia de ocho horas. Grupo de instituto de Santa Bárbara que había hecho folk rock en Gold Star, se rehízo a comienzos de 1966 animado a «viajar por el bien de la banda»; el guitarrista Bruce Clawson tradujo su asombro y su terror en un formato pop. El título viene del best seller de Lobsang Rampa (en realidad Cyril Hoskin, de Devon), que también usaron Dylan y los 13th Floor Elevators de Austin, formados expresamente para difundir la conciencia LSD. Aquellos primeros discos de ácido no eran beatíficos sino crudos, salvajes y amenazantes: «The Trip» de Kim Fowley, «Ain’t It Hard» de los Gypsy Trips, «Free Advice» de The Great!! Society!!. Sin una gran discográfica detrás, «The Third Eye» cayó en el vacío, y Clawson oyó «Eight Miles High» en la radio unas semanas después.

notes.chapter: Septiembre: 7 And 7 Is: provocaciones, sombras y un nuevo lenguaje
notes.text: «You’re Gonna Miss Me» de los 13th Floor Elevators, con la burbuja electrónica de la jarra eléctrica de Tommy Hall, era un caballo de Troya de la revolución psicodélica: una canción de despecho adolescente que predicaba el LSD («look around in your mind»). Hall convenció al grupo de tocar en ácido para contagiar el viaje al público; cuatro de ellos fueron detenidos en enero de 1966 en Texas.

notes.chapter: Diciembre: My Mind’s Eye: sueños de libertad, una minoría profética y el regreso a la infancia
notes.text: En diciembre salió The Psychedelic Sounds of the 13th Floor Elevators, con un Tercer Ojo en la portada y notas de Tommy Hall como guía del ácido («esta búsqueda de la cordura pura»): la guitarra de Stacy Sutherland, la jarra de Hall y los gritos de Roky Erickson en «Roller Coaster», «Reverberation» y «Fire Engine». Mal distribuido, pasó casi inadvertido. Los Blues Magoos de Nueva York sacaron Psychedelic Lollipop.

refs.q: Released in April 1966, the Dovers’ ‘The Third Eye’ is one of the earliest attempts at reproducing the LSD experience on record
refs.para: Released in April 1966, the Dovers’ ‘The Third Eye’ is one of the earliest attempts at reproducing the LSD experience on record; it’s also one of the most accurate expressions of how this extraordinarily powerful drug impacted on the consciousness of those teens who took it in late 1965 and early 1966. Like many early acid records, it is not beatific – that would be a later gloss – but raw, wild and threatening.
refs.chapter: Abril: The Third Eye: el LSD y sus descontentos

refs.q: ‘The Third Eye’ was a lightning strike.
refs.para: ‘The Third Eye’ was a lightning strike. Based in Santa Barbara, about ninety miles from Hollywood, the Dovers had formed as a high-school group inspired by frat rock and the British invasion. They recorded a couple of superior folk rock records at Gold Star Studios during 1965 – the teen janglers ‘Your Love’ and ‘I Could Be Happy’ – which were released on the small Hollywood Miramar label. ‘I Could Be Happy’ was quickly picked up by Reprise Records, but that didn’t break the group nationally.
refs.chapter: Abril: The Third Eye: el LSD y sus descontentos

refs.q: In 1966, ‘mind’ was a keyword that spoke of hallucinogenic drugs
refs.para: Thirteen places below the Standells was another young group with a harsh, arresting single. On the surface, the 13th Floor Elevators’ ‘You’re Gonna Miss Me’ was a revenge song in the teen romance mode, just like ‘96 Tears’. Yet the performance and the record’s whole ambience spoke of something completely different, with its slashing chords, plunging melody and an intense, rasping vocal that broke into testifying screams. The hook was the strange reverberation that resonated through the record, a primitive electronic bubble that was both a signature and a challenge. In the first verse, the singer gives the clue: ‘You’re gonna look around in your mind, girl / You’re gonna find that I’m gone.’ In 1966, ‘mind’ was a keyword that spoke of hallucinogenic drugs, and ‘You’re Gonna Miss Me’ was a Trojan Horse for the psychedelic revolution, a teen romance song that proselytised LSD.
refs.chapter: Septiembre: 7 And 7 Is: provocaciones, sombras y un nuevo lenguaje

refs.q: The 13th Floor Elevators had three unique facets
refs.para: The 13th Floor Elevators had three unique facets: Stacy Sutherland’s ringing guitar – a psychedelicised Buddy Holly; Tommy Hall’s jug, which created an almost mechanical, pulsing drone in the background; and Roky Erickson’s voice, which could switch from R&B testifying to an other-worldly shriek, as if something had possessed his soul. With this armoury, they inhabited the LSD experience in songs like the wildly bucking ‘Roller Coaster’, the paranoid ‘Reverberation’ and the sheer velocity of ‘Fire Engine’, a drug rush incarnate.

podcast.title: Origins of the Word "Psychedelic" – Coined 1956 by Psychiatrist Humphrey Osmond; Means "Soul-Revealing" in Greek
podcast.body: The word "psychedelic" was coined in 1956 by British psychiatrist Humphrey Osmond, who was studying pharmaceuticals including LSD (Lysergic Acid Diethylamide, first synthesized from the ergot fungus by Swiss scientist Albert Hofmann in 1943 and marketed commercially for a period under the brand name Delysid). The CIA also studied LSD for potential use in interrogation, chemical warfare, and mind control. As the drugs spread recreationally, artists took notice and the word became an adjective for anything mind-expanding. "Psychedelic means soul revealing in Greek."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: A Brief History of Alt Psychedelic Rock

podcast.title: Beatles' "Tomorrow Never Knows" (1966) – Blueprint for Psychedelic Music
podcast.body: The Beatles' "Tomorrow Never Knows" from Revolver (1966) contains all the elements that defined early psychedelic music: drug references, an unusual rhythm track, sitar drone, backwards tape, sound effects, and samples. By 1966 the Beatles were deep into the drug culture that had lived in the jazz and folk world for years, incorporating their time in India with Maharishi Mahesh Yogi and their use of LSD. The Beach Boys' Pet Sounds (1966), Jefferson Airplane's "White Rabbit," the 13th Floor Elevators' album The Psychedelic Sounds of the 13th Floor Elevators, early Pink Floyd (including "Interstellar Overdrive," 1967), and the Velvet Underground (playing Andy Warhol happenings) all followed in this tradition. "That track has everything psychedelic music would need to get started."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: A Brief History of Alt Psychedelic Rock

podcast.title: Early Rock Subdivision (Pre-1977)
podcast.body: Psychedelic rock, referred to as "psych," was identified as one of the multitude of different directions that rock music had grown into by 1977, signifying an early and distinct subgenre within the broader rock landscape. "Rock had already grown in a multitude of different directions, metal, Prague, psych, and the so-called corporate rock bands like Boston and Kansas."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 2: (90-81)

podcast.title: Contemporary Neo-Psych (2000s–Present) – Flaming Lips, Original Scream, Animal Collective, Tame Impala
podcast.body: By the 2000s, neo-psychedelia had dispersed across many sounds united more by effect than style. Artists frequently described as psychedelic include the Flaming Lips, MGMT (their druggy danceable psychedelia), Elephant Six (Colorado label specializing in psych flavors), Super Furry Animals, The Black Angels, Animal Collective, Mercury Rev, and Arctic Monkeys (certain songs). Oasis's drone-heavy "Do You Know What I Mean?" has psych elements. Australian artist Tame Impala (Kevin Parker, Perth, Western Australia) has had international alt-rock hits with modern psych, including "Elephant" from the 2012 album Lonerism. "By the time we get to the 2000s, Neosychedelia had taken on all kinds of new dimensions."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: A Brief History of Alt Psychedelic Rock

podcast.title: Decline in Popularity (Early 1970s)
podcast.body: In the early 1970s, many music fans abandoned the "mind-blowing acid rock" of the 1960s, opting instead for a softer, "Mellow" sound, reflecting a shift in musical tastes. "Many fans had deserted the mind-blowing acid rock and the hard-driving funk and the soulful R&B of the 60s and decided to go all soft."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence on Glam
podcast.body: The remnants of psychedelic music, particularly its distorted and eccentric guitar sounds (exemplified by Syd Barrett), were a key influence on the development of glam rock. "En gran medida se basaban en los restos en la música psicodélica, de gente como podía ser sin barred de la quereda, esa guitarra tan distorsionada y a veces es un tanto excéntrica."

srcs.episode: EL PIONERO DEL GLAM: MARC BOLAN Y T REX

podcast.title: Key Characteristics of Psychedelic Music
podcast.body: Psych music shares several common traits regardless of era: exotic instruments (Indian sitar and tabla), dreamy jams, disjointed song structures with unusual time signature changes, the drone (a sustained note or chord underpinning the music), and surreal lyrics that resist straightforward interpretation. The effect — not any single sound — is what unifies the genre. "There is no one psychedelic sound, there's no one style, but you know it when you hear it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: A Brief History of Alt Psychedelic Rock

podcast.title: Kula Shaker – Crispin Mills, Son of Hayley Mills; Deeply Into Psych and Hinduism
podcast.body: British band Kula Shaker, formed 1995, had a substantial alt-rock radio hit in the late 1990s with "Tattva." Frontman Crispin Mills is the son of actress Hayley Mills (Disney films, 1960s). Mills is deeply involved in psychedelia to the point of adopting the spiritual name Krishna Kanta Das. "The singer there is Crispin Mills, he's the son of Haley Mills."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: A Brief History of Alt Psychedelic Rock

podcast.title: Late 1960s UK Dominance
podcast.body: In the late 1960s, psychedelic rock, alongside progressive music, heavily dominated the music scene in the United Kingdom. This genre was characterized by its highly elaborate, worked, and perfectionist musical approach. "la música en el reino nido está dominada por el roxico delico y la música progresiva, era música muy recargada, muy trabajada, muy perfeccionista."

srcs.episode: EL PIONERO DEL GLAM: MARC BOLAN Y T REX

podcast.title: Neo-Psychedelic Rock (Late 1970s–Early 1980s) – British Post-Punk Branches
podcast.body: When the first wave of psychedelic music was discredited by establishment reaction to acid casualties and the counterculture's failures (Manson murders, etc.), its spirit survived through 1970s prog rock and Krautrock. Post-punk reactivated it as neo-psychedelia: a blend of jangly guitars (George Harrison–style 12-string), keyboards and synthesizers, long experimental jams, and mandatory drug allusions. Three British bands formed the holy trinity of neo-psych pioneers: The Soft Boys (featuring Robin Hitchcock; album A Can of Bees, 1979), The Teardrop Explodes (featuring Julian Cope; album Kilimanjaro, 1980, seven singles), and Echo and the Bunnymen (Liverpool, 1978; led by Ian McCullough and Will Sergeant; multiple top-10 UK singles; "Bring On the Dancing Horses" placed on the Pretty in Pink soundtrack by John Hughes). "This has been called Neo-psychedelic rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: A Brief History of Alt Psychedelic Rock

podcast.title: Peak During 1960s Societal Upheaval
podcast.body: Acid rock, along with electric rock, reached its peak popularity during the "general upheaval of society in the 1960s." Its subsequent decline in the 1970s mirrored a broader societal mellowing. "The general upheaval of society in the 1960s has passed when acid rock and electric rock were peaking."

srcs.episode: Ep. 51 - The Softer Side of 70s Rock
Ep. 51 - The Softer Side of 70s Rock

podcast.title: Revival in the Mid-2010s
podcast.body: Various flavors of psychedelic music experienced a revival period around the mid-2010s, indicating a recurring interest in the genre's sounds and aesthetics. "About a decade later, there was another revival. Straight ahead, punk came back into fashion as did emo, shoegays, and various flavors of psychedelic music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 2: (90-81)

podcast.title: Rise and Attitudes
podcast.body: Psychedelic rock rose in the late 1960s, known for its "trippy attitudes" and experimental nature. "we had the rise of psychedelic rock in its trippy attitudes."

podcast.title: Shoegaze (Late 1980s–Early 1990s) – My Bloody Valentine, Chapterhouse, Ride, Lush
podcast.body: A British psych derivative characterized by floaty, fuzzy, drony music designed to overload the senses — often through sheer volume — creating a warm, enveloping bath of sound. My Bloody Valentine's Loveless (1991) is considered the genre's masterwork, inspiring a wave of followers including Chapterhouse, Ride, and Lush. "Floty, fuzzy, drony music that often felt like a warm bath with its attempts to overload the senses often through sheer volume."

podcast.title: Siouxsie and the Banshees and Psych – John McGeoch's Swirly Guitar
podcast.body: Though most often grouped with Goth, Siouxsie and the Banshees took a significant psychedelic turn after guitarist John McGeoch joined in 1980. A 1983 cover of the Beatles' "Dear Prudence" (from the Beatles' most psychedelic phase, inspired by time in India and LSD use) exemplifies the swirly, trippy guitar work that made McGeoch one of alt rock's most influential guitarists. "John has gone down in history as being one of alt rocks more interesting and influential guitarists."

podcast.title: Space Rock (Early 1990s) – The Verve; Pink Floyd Update with Heavy Reverb
podcast.body: Following shoegaze, a related strand labeled "space rock" featured heavy reverb, multiple layers of distorted guitars, and relaxed, almost cosmic drumming — an update on what Pink Floyd did in the late 1960s. The Verve (before the legal dispute over their name) exemplified this on their debut album A Storm in Heaven (1993). "It's kind of like an update in what Pink Floyd was about in the late 1960s."

podcast.title: Spacemen 3 (UK, Mid-1980s) – "Taking Drugs to Make Music to Take Drugs To"
podcast.body: Spacemen 3 were categorized as a drug band because members openly and enthusiastically discussed their regular drug use. Their early demos were released under the title Taking Drugs to Make Music to Take Drugs To, which was their stated mission. They promoted what they called "minimalist psychedelia": one or two chords often sufficed, and the drone was central to the effect. Active on the UK indie charts from the mid-to-late 1980s, they split into two projects when the band dissolved — co-frontman Jason Pierce went on to form Spiritualized. "Their early demos were issued under the title, Taking Drugs to Make Music To Take Drugs To."

podcast.title: The Paisley Underground (Los Angeles) – Jangly 12-String Guitars; The Bangles, R.E.M., Tom Petty
podcast.body: In Los Angeles in the early 1980s, a scene called the Paisley Underground blended classic rock (birds, Byrds, post-Beatles George Harrison), the Doors, Creedence Clearwater Revival, and post-punk alternative into jangly, 12-string guitar-driven psychedelic pop. The Bangles emerged from this scene, beginning as a mamas-and-papas-influenced pop-psych post-punk band. This jangly-guitar approach was also enormously influential on R.E.M. (their first half-dozen records) and Tom Petty. "This was a sound dominated by jangly guitars, reminiscent of the kind of music played by groups like the birds and the hallies."
